sources.title: Amir Khusrau (Q207817), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-31): English description 'Indian poet, writer, singer and scholar (1253-1325)', born 1253 (year-level precision), died 1325-09-27, country India, Korean label present, image 'Amir Khusraw (portrait) presents a book of poetry to Ala'uddin Khalji' from the Smithsonian. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Annemarie Schimmel, 'Amir Khosrow Dehlavi', Encyclopaedia Iranica (1989), read in full. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the 'Parrot of India', the greatest Persian-writing poet of medieval India; served the family of Sultan Balban and later the Khalji and Tughluq rulers, writing most of his works under Ala al-Din Khalji; a significant contribution to the development of the ghazal in India; the five-poem Khamsa written between 1298 and 1301 in imitation of Nizami but, in the author's judgement, lacking the flavour of Nizami's work; a new genre of historical epic; the nine-meter Noh Sepehr (1318); prose including the epistolography treatise Ijaz-e Khosravi; attachment from 1272 to the Chishti saint Nizam al-Din Awliya; a warning that he is 'praised as having invented Hindustani music' with none of his work in the field preserved, and that the authenticity of the Hindi fragments ascribed to him is still discussed. Scholarly encyclopedia entry; the main limit on what can be scored.

Iraj Bashiri, 'Amir Khusrau Dihlavi', Persian literature pages (University of Minnesota), read in full: born at Patiali in 1253 of a Turkic father and an Indian mother, fluent in Persian and familiar with Arabic, Hindi and Sanskrit, drawn to Nizami's poetry, a disciple of the Chishti shaykh Nizam al-Din, a listing of his five divans and nine mathnavis, and the statement that he invented the sitar, which conflicts with the scholarly caution in the other sources here. Short professor's overview with English verse translations; calls two of his Nizami imitations poor, and its sitar claim is not used.

Malini Nair, 'Seven Centuries on, Delhi Is Still Resounding with the Legacy of Amir Khusrau' (Scroll.in, reprinted by Janata Weekly), read in full: he wrote for the sultans of Delhi, five of whom he served, as well as for his Sufi master, mixing Persian with Braj Bhasha and Khadi Boli; the scholar Sunil Sharma describes his influence on Indian-Islamic cultural traditions and notes that he documented none of the musical achievements attributed to him, with the stories that he created the khayal and invented the sitar and tabla being oral tradition; Katherine Schofield says he did not invent the khayal, though his legacy lay behind it; Jahangir's memoir records a qawwali with a Khusrau verse as refrain. Cultural journalism quoting scholars; the main independent and critical voice on the musical claims.

Nizamuddin Aulia Dargah, 'Hazrat Amir Khusrau' biography page, read in full: educated in literature, fiqh, astronomy, grammar, philosophy and history, fluent in Persian, Arabic and Turkish and several Indian dialects, appointed court poet in 1272, served several rulers while remaining a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, and is buried beside him; it also tells a devotional story of how he became the saint's disciple. Shrine's own page, devotional in tone, so the anecdote is excluded and the page is used only for the dated service record.

Sufinama (Rekhta Foundation), 'Profile of Amir Khusrau', read in full: lists the princes and rulers he served, calls him soldier, courtier, Sufi, poet and musician, and says that 'the number of his works cannot be ascertained for sure, nor can the authenticity of works ascribed to him be determined with any confidence', while repeating that he invented the tabla and sitar. Literary-foundation profile; admiring and partly traditional, used only for its own caution about attribution.

Art Institute of Chicago, object page and data record for 'Amir Khusrau Dedicates His Poem to Sultan Ala al-Din Khalji, page from the Quintet (Khamsa) of Amir Khusraw Dehlavi' (accession 1962.640), read: anonymous Indian painting of the Delhi Sultanate period, mid-fifteenth century, opaque watercolour and ink on paper, the museum's data flagged public domain and released under a Creative Commons Zero designation. Used only for the portrait.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_khusrau_iranica, src_khusrau_scroll | c.1272-1325 | scholarly encyclopedia, cultural journalism quoting scholars] Iranica documents several distinct innovations: a significant contribution to bringing the ghazal into Indian use, a new genre of historical epic (Qiran al-Sa'dain, 1289, and the Meftah al-Fotuh poem on Jalal al-Din Khalji's victories), and Noh Sepehr (1318), in which nine spheres are set in nine different meters; Sunil Sharma, quoted by Scroll, credits him with helping form Indian-Islamic cultural traditions and the Hindavi vernacular. Counter-voices limit the row: Iranica judges the Khamsa an imitation without Nizami's flavour, Bashiri calls two of the imitations poor, and the musical inventions credited to him are undocumented, so the score rests on the literary contributions only.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_khusrau_iranica, src_khusrau_scroll, src_khusrau_dargah | c.1272-1325 | scholarly encyclopedia, cultural journalism, shrine page] Iranica calls him musician and scholar who wrote lyric poetry, epics and prose on epistolography and the campaigns of Ala al-Din Khalji, in Persian with Hindi play, and notes his attachment to the Chishti master Nizam al-Din; Scroll lists him as poet, musician, Sufi, chronicler and courtier; the shrine page lists a wide education from fiqh to astronomy. The literary range across lyric, epic, chronicle prose and wordplay in several languages is well documented, but the musical part is traditional and undocumented. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as a top-risk row; lowered from 66 / 0.52 to 62 / 0.48 because the musician side rests on traditions that Iranica and Sharma say are not documented.

adaptability.rationale: [src_khusrau_iranica, src_khusrau_dargah, src_khusrau_sufinama | 1272-1325 | scholarly encyclopedia, shrine page, literary profile] Iranica and the two profiles agree that he kept his place as court poet through several changes of ruling house and patron, from Balban's family through the Khalji and Tughluq reigns, and Iranica adds that this was normal practice for medieval poets in a confused period. The record shows continuity of professional position, but not his own reasons or any specific change of method, so the row is a modest inference. Political roles and conquests are not scored.

execution_speed.rationale: [src_khusrau_iranica | 1298-1301, 1318 | scholarly encyclopedia] Iranica dates the five mathnavis of the Khamsa to between 698/1298 and 701/1301 and says he wrote them 'with great ease', and adds that he collected several divans at dated intervals and produced epics, prose treatises and chronicle prose across the 1290s-1320. The dating is from one source and the 'ease' is the writer's own characterisation, so the confidence is low; the quality of the Khamsa is judged below Nizami's by the same source, and speed is not credited as a virtue here.

portrait.reason: The only rights-clear image found is an imagined mid-15th-century court-scene miniature (Art Institute of Chicago 1962.640, open access) in which the poet is one of several figures and is not singled out; the lead's first lead, a Freer Gallery folio, carries a live Smithsonian 'Usage Conditions Apply' notice that conflicts with the Commons PD tag. Without a positively identified single figure it cannot be presented as a portrait of Amir Khusrau. Next step: a captioned single-figure depiction with an item-level open licence (for example a manuscript miniature whose caption names him), or written permission from a holder.

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: strong (lead) / FAILED on the lead's file, REPLACED by a clearer one. The lead's Commons file (Smithsonian Freer|Sackler S1986.213, 'Amir Khusraw presents a book to Ala'uddin Khalji', Balkh 1503-04) is tagged PD-Art on Commons, but the live National Museum of Asian Art object page (asia.si.edu/object/S1986.213) says under Restrictions and Rights 'Usage Conditions Apply. There are restrictions for re-using this media', not CC0, and the Commons date field also reads '~1525' against the museum's 1503-1504; a generic Commons tag does not override the institution's own notice, so it was rejected. One bounded retry: from the Commons category I picked 'Anonymous - Amir Khusraw Dedicates His Poem to Sultan Ala al-Din Khalji' (Art Institute of Chicago 1962.640). The AIC data record (api.artic.edu/api/v1/artworks/14848) says is_public_domain true, no copyright notice, anonymous Indian painting, date 1400-1466, and states that its data is released under CC0; the AIC open-access page says images of works believed to be in the public domain are offered under a CC0 designation with a requested caption (Artist. Title, Date. The Art Institute of Chicago), which the attribution uses. The Commons page for the same file also shows PD-old plus CC0, consistent with the museum. The anonymous work is far older than any term of protection, so the basis is age, with the museum's CC0 designation as confirmation. The IIIF image is 2204 x 3000 pixels (info.json); the server refused the full-size render, so I used its 1200 x 1633 rendering and cropped the miniature to 965 x 440 (viewed: five figures in a court scene, no text). Honest limit: this is a scene, not a portrait, and the museum names the scene but does not mark which figure is the poet, so it is kind historical_depiction and a weak identification; the Smithsonian folio is the same type of scene. The tag 'mystic' was not used because Iranica says a Sufi flavour is hard to detect in his writings. KO NAME: Wikidata Korean label 아미르 호스로우. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Annemarie Schimmel, 'Amir Khosrow Dehlavi', Encyclopaedia Iranica (https://iranicaonline.org/articles/amir-kosrow-poet). READ IN FULL: Iranica, Bashiri, Scroll/Janata, the Nizamuddin dargah page, the Sufinama profile (five sources) plus the AIC object record for the portrait. PERSPECTIVES: scholarly encyclopedia, university professor's overview, cultural journalism quoting two scholars, shrine, literary foundation. COUNTER-VOICES: Iranica's judgment of the Khamsa and its caution on 'invented Hindustani music' and on the Hindi fragments; Sharma and Schofield in the Scroll article on the musical claims; Sufinama's own caution on attribution. NOT OPENED: Britannica (blocked), Sunil Sharma's biography and Mohammad Habib's and Wahid Mirza's studies (known only through citations), Ziauddin Barani, Khusrau's own divan prefaces and Khazain al-Futuh (self-report in any case), the Smithsonian image file, the Rana Safvi article (returned no text). CONFLICTS: Bashiri and Sufinama state he invented the sitar and tabla while Iranica and the Scroll scholars say the claims are undocumented, so no row and no card states them; Sufinama gives 1252 for his birth and Wikidata 1253 (the Iranica and other sources year is used). EXCLUDED: the devotional anecdotes about meeting Nizamuddin and the Basant story, the 'father of qawwali' and 'father of Urdu' labels, his campaigns and conquest chronicles as evidence of military traits, and any reading of his temperament from his poems. SELF-GATE (first pass): all five checks PASS; card 1 states the defining contribution (the greatest Persian-writing poet of medieval India, a Delhi court poet whose lyric, epic and prose work shaped Indo-Persian literature), card 2 the Khamsa and the historical epics, card 3 the Hindavi and Sufi/qawwali legacy with its documentation limit.
